title: FIDE Statement on the Conclusion of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026
summary: Following the conclusion of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 in Budapest, the International Chess Federation (FIDE) congratulates the medalists, GMs Alireza Firouzja, Anish Giri, and Fabiano Caruana. FIDE also extends its thanks to Kjell Madland, the entire Total Chess team, and the Hungarian hosts for organizing this important pilot event ahead of the inaugural full season of the Tour in 2027. At the same time, FIDE expresses serious concern over several instances of players forfeiting scheduled games during the tournament. Some of these forfeits, including those by GM Magnus Carlsen, occurred in matches whose outcomes had already been mathematically decided. Although such actions breached the tournament regulations requiring all scheduled games to be played, they did not affect the results of the respective matches. However, GM Magnus Carlsen also forfeited three scheduled games over two days of his match against GM Vladislav Artemiev while the outcomes of the respective contests were still undecided. Such repeated misconduct undermines the principles of fair play and the fairness of the competition and is unprecedented at the highest level of professional chess. These forfeited games were highly significant, seriously impacting the very top of the rating standings. FIDE considers such conduct unacceptable and inconsistent with the standards of professional behavior expected of participants in official competitions. Given GM Carlsen’s stature and his significant role in promoting chess, such actions are particularly concerning, as they may damage the reputation of competitions and demonstrate a lack of respect for opponents, spectators, and tournament partners. Accordingly, FIDE will refer the relevant materials to the FIDE Ethics and Disciplinary Commission (EDC) for an independent assessment of potential violations of the FIDE Ethics and Disciplinary Code. Furthermore, the officiating during the event fell short of fundamental standards, as the arbiters effectively abdicated their responsibility to uphold the FIDE Laws of Chess and tournament regulations. Consequently, the actions of the arbiters involved will be referred to the FIDE Arbiters’ Commission (ARB) and its Disciplinary Sub-Committee (DSC) for thorough examination and assessment. As the Budapest event was intended to test the competition format and regulations ahead of the 2027 season, FIDE will continue working closely with Total Chess to refine the rules governing player forfeits and their consequences, thereby preventing similar incidents in the future. FIDE reaffirms its commitment to ensuring that all official competitions are conducted in accordance with the principles of fairness, sporting integrity, and respect for all participants. Timur TurlovFIDE President Viswanathan AnandFIDE Deputy President

additionalSources.title: FIDE Calls Carlsen's Forfeits 'Unacceptable,' Refers His Conduct To Ethics Commission
additionalSources.summary:
FIDE will refer GM Magnus Carlsen's conduct at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot to its Ethics and Disciplinary Commission (EDC), describing his forfeits as "unacceptable.” The tournament’s arbiters will also face a separate review of their handling of the incidents.

The statement, published on Saturday and signed by FIDE president Timur Turlov and its deputy president GM Viswanathan Anand, follows five forfeited games by Carlsen over the final four days in Budapest. The world number-one finished 17th after skipping Friday's fast classical game against GM Vladislav Artemiev, then winning the deciding armageddon game.

Timur Turlov FIDE President Viswanathan Anand FIDE Deputy President 📷 Total Chess / Michal Walusza

— International Chess Federation (@FIDE_chess) November 21, 2026

FIDE noted the difference between skipping games after a match was already decided, such as against GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, and Carlsen’s three forfeits against Artemiev: two rapid games on Thursday and the fast classical game on Friday.

"Such repeated misconduct undermines the principles of fair play and the fairness of the competition and is unprecedented at the highest level of professional chess," they noted about his forfeits against Artemiev.

Such repeated misconduct undermines the principles of fair play and the fairness of the competition and is unprecedented at the highest level of professional chess.

—FIDE statement

"FIDE considers such conduct unacceptable and inconsistent with the standards of professional behavior expected of participants in official competitions," the statement continued.

"Given GM Carlsen’s stature and his significant role in promoting chess, such actions are particularly concerning, as they may damage the reputation of competitions and demonstrate a lack of respect for opponents, spectators, and tournament partners."

FIDE also said the forfeited games had seriously affected the top of the rating standings. Unplayed games do not affect a player’s rating, meaning Carlsen’s forfeits avoided the rating risk of playing them.

Magnus Carlsen eventually won the match against Vladislav Artemiev. Photo: Total Chess.

With the case now being referred to the EDC for an independent review, Carlsen could face a disciplinary sanction, including a warning, a fine, or a suspension, if the EDC finds that he breached its code.

He has previously been sanctioned by the commission. In December 2023, the EDC fined him €10,000 for withdrawing without valid reason from the 2022 Sinquefield Cup following his loss to GM Hans Niemann. He was cleared of the three other charges in that case.

Carlsen is not the only one who could face repercussions. FIDE is also critical of the arbiters' conduct at the event, saying they had "effectively abdicated their responsibility to uphold the FIDE Laws of Chess and tournament regulations." Their actions have been referred to the FIDE Arbiters’ Commission and its Disciplinary Sub-Committee.

Carlsen also received criticism from several of his fellow grandmasters during the event. One of them was GM Fabiano Caruana, who said:

"I don't think it's good at all. I don't think it was good the first time... but this is even worse because you are leaving in the middle of the match. I think you should just forfeit the match if you don't play,” he told ChessBase India.

He later made a tennis comparison.

"To me, its like in Tennis someone decided to drop the 2nd set and come back for the 3rd set. I don't think I've seen anything like this in chess or any other sport!" - Fabiano Caruana on Magnus Carlsen not playing the Fast Classic game against Artemiev. https://t.co/JfNZQd2XFq

— ChessBase India (@ChessbaseIndia) November 21, 2026

GM Ian Nepomniachtchi went further, calling for Carlsen's removal from the event. "I think the player has to be expelled from the tournament," he said, also describing the conduct as "disrespect."

GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave described the tournament as a worthwhile experiment, but added: "I’m a bit sad that some of the players decided to make their own headlines."

Vachier-Lagrave then sharpened that criticism in a reply on X, apparently referring to Carlsen:

Correction: that a crybaby decided to make his own headlines.

— MVL (@Vachier_Lagrave) November 20, 2026

GM Levon Aronian shared a different perspective. "This event did make me melancholic and sad, but people change and sometimes not for better,” he wrote on X. "For people who are disappointed with Magnus Carlsen i want you to see his actions as a blessing for chess."

Happy to finish Total Chess Pilot. My play was not great, but it was first time we played 45+30 time control and I got to like it, even though i think 15 minutes after move 40 would greatly improve the quality of the games and still keep it exciting. Congrats to @AlirezaFirouzja and @anishgiri (especially!!) for showing amazing skills and my old buddies @FabianoCaruana and @Vachier_Lagrave for being their usual great! This event did make me melancholic and sad,but people change and sometimes not for better. For people who are disappointed with @MagnusCarlsen i want you to see his actions as a blessing for chess. New generation plays hard and shows their hunger. Look them in the eyes, they are exceptional players, intelligent and kind people. We have a world of potential and i feel that the players have the full support to make positive changes in every aspect of the game. What else do we need?

— Levon Aronian (@LevAronian) November 21, 2026

Former FIDE presidential candidate and tournament organizer Wadim Rosenstein defended Carlsen, arguing that the controversy exposed problems with the tournament’s incentives as well as questions of individual responsibility.

"I stand firmly in defence of Magnus Carlsen following the controversy at the Total Chess pilot tournament in Budapest," he wrote on X.

Rosenstein said Assaubayeva deserved an opponent and proper communication, and acknowledged the reported instruction that all scheduled games had to be played. But he questioned a system in which a player who had already secured the result could lose rating points by drawing the remaining game, while forfeiting it carried no rating cost.

"Why did the tournament regulations create a situation in which not playing was more beneficial than playing?" he asked.

I stand firmly in defence of Magnus Carlsen following the controversy at the Total Chess pilot tournament in Budapest. When senior FIDE officials, including Deputy President Anand and Advisor Sutovsky, publicly criticised Magnus for missing scheduled games, they raised legitimate questions about sporting responsibility. Anand questioned Carlsen’s decision while also acknowledging that the tournament regulations needed improvement. Sutovsky went further, publicly describing his conduct as “pathetic” and “unsportsmanlike.” Every player who sits down at the board deserves an opponent. Bibisara certainly deserved that respect, and I believe Magnus should have ensured she was informed of his decision. However, I believe we are overlooking a much bigger problem. Why did the tournament regulations create a situation in which not playing was more beneficial than playing? By the time Magnus was scheduled to face Bibisara, he had already won their match. According to the chief arbiter’s explanation, he consulted the arbiters before the game. Forfeiting the remaining game would count as a loss in the match but would not affect his classical rating. Had he played and drawn, he would still have won the match but would have lost rating points because of the rating difference. Think about that. The regulations effectively created an incentive for a player to stay away from the board rather than compete. Magnus later missed two rapid games against Vladislav and acknowledged that rating considerations influenced his decision. I am not suggesting that every decision Magnus made was correct. Nor am I ignoring the reported instruction that all scheduled games were expected to be played. But if tournament regulations create incentives that contradict the fundamental principles of sporting competition, we must examine those regulations rather than focus exclusively on criticising individual players. And this brings me to another important issue. I call upon senior FIDE officials, including Mr Anand and Mr Sutovsky, to demonstrate neutrality, professionalism and institutional responsibility. Of course, officials are entitled to personal opinions. But when someone holds a senior position in an international sports federation, their public statements carry additional weight. I find it concerning when senior officials publicly criticise athletes over controversies arising from competitions within the international chess system without placing sufficient emphasis on examining the underlying regulations. Public criticism of individual athletes should never become a substitute for institutional accountability. title: Casablanca and Oromana take early lead at Spanish Team Championship
summary:
MyInvestor Casablanca and Oromana Cen Solutions are the only teams to have won both their matches after two rounds of the Spanish Team Championship in Marbella. Casablanca lead the standings on tiebreaks following a convincing 5–1 victory over Silla Bosch Serinsys, while Oromana edged out Jaime Casas de Monzón. The eight-team competition features a strong international field, including Nihal Sarin, Parham Maghsoodloo (pictured), Nodirbek Yakubboev and Alexei Shirov. | Photo: Spanish Chess Federation

Two teams remain perfect

The 2026 Spanish Team Chess Championship (División de Honor) is taking place from 20 to 26 November at the Alanda Hotel in Marbella, Málaga. Eight clubs are competing in the country's top team competition, with seven rounds scheduled over seven consecutive days.

The championship follows a single round-robin format, with each encounter played over six boards. Teams receive 2 match points for a victory and 1 for a draw, while individual game points serve as the first tiebreak criterion. The time control is 90 minutes for 40 moves, followed by 30 additional minutes, with a 30-second increment from move one. The bottom two teams will be relegated to the First Division (Primera División).

The lineups include a number of strong international grandmasters. The highest-rated registered player is India's Nihal Sarin (2720), representing Duobeniajan Costa Cálida. He is followed by Iran's Parham Maghsoodloo (2705) and Uzbekistan's Nodirbek Yakubboev (2701), both playing for Oromana Cen Solutions.

Other notable participants include Aydin Suleymanli, Pranav Venkatesh, Pranesh M, Haik Martirosyan, Pavel Eljanov and Volodar Murzin. The Spanish contingent features Alexei Shirov, Francisco Vallejo, Jaime Santos and David Antón, while young Argentine talent Faustino Oro is part of the MyInvestor Casablanca squad.

The competition also features several prominent female players, including Nana Dzagnidze, Nino Batsiashvili, Sarasadat Khademalsharieh and Stavroula Tsolakidou. Each team's line-up must include at least one female player.

Ann Matnadze Bujiashvili is playing for FCC Medio Ambiente Benalmádena | Photo: Spanish Chess Federation

The opening round saw MyInvestor Casablanca defeat Filántropos Equigoma 4–2, with Ediz Gürel, Pranav Anand and Javier Habans scoring wins. Oromana Cen Solutions also made a winning start, edging out Duobeniaján Costa Cálida 3½–2½ thanks to victories by Yakubboev and Alan Pichot.

Casablanca and Oromana maintained their perfect records in round two. Casablanca scored a convincing 5–1 victory over Silla, with Gürel, Vallejo, Habans and Sabrina Vega all winning their games. Oromana had a tougher encounter against Jaime Casas de Monzón, securing a 3½–2½ victory thanks to wins by Maghsoodloo and Khademalsharieh.
